claim: Two rhesus monkeys conducted instructed walk-and-reach movements towards targets flexibly positioned in the cage.
source: Two rhesus monkeys conducted instructed walk-and-reach movements towards targets flexibly positioned in the cage.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by behavioral data showing task performance.

claim: Movements show small trial-to-trial variability despite being unrestrained.
source: Movements show small trial-to-trial variability despite being unrestrained.
evidence: Supported by kinematic analysis showing median deviations and standard deviations in movement trajectories.

claim: 192 broad-band neural signals were wirelessly recorded from three cortical sensorimotor areas simultaneously.
source: We wirelessly recorded 192 broad-band neural signals from three cortical sensorimotor areas simultaneously.
evidence: Directly stated and supported by methods describing the recording setup with six 32-channel arrays.

claim: Single unit activity is selective for different reach and walk-and-reach movements.
source: Single unit activity is selective for different reach and walk-and-reach movements.
evidence: Supported by example units showing task-related modulation and ANOVA results.

claim: Walk-and-reach targets could be decoded from premotor and parietal but not motor cortical activity during movement planning.
source: Walk-and-reach targets could be decoded from premotor and parietal but not motor cortical activity during movement planning.
evidence: Supported by SVM decoding analysis showing significant decoding accuracy in PMd and PRR but not M1 during the memory period.

claim: The primate frontoparietal network encodes reach goals beyond immediate reach during movement planning.
source: We conclude that the primate frontoparietal network encodes reach goals beyond immediate reach during movement planning.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from decoding analysis showing target information in PMd and PRR during memory period for far targets.

claim: The frontoparietal reach network includes the posterior parietal cortex, premotor cortex, and motor cortex.
source: The frontoparietal reach network, in particular, including the posterior parietal cortex, premotor cortex, and motor cortex, has been studied in terms of force encoding (Cheney and Fetz, 1980), direction encoding (Georgopoulos et al., 1986), spatial reference frames of reach goal encoding (Batista et al., 1999; Buneo et al., 2002; Kuang et al., 2016; Pesaran et al., 2006), context integration (Gail and Andersen, 2006; Martínez-Vázquez and Gail, 2018; Niebergall et al., 2011; Westendorff et al., 2010), obstacle avoidance (Kaufman et al., 2013; Mulliken et al., 2008), bimanual coordination (Donchin et al., 1998; Mooshagian et al., 2018), eye-hand coordination (Hwang et al., 2012; Mooshagian and Snyder, 2018; Sayegh et al., 2017; Wong et al., 2016), and decision making (Christopoulos et al., 2015; Cisek, 2012; Klaes et al., 2011; Suriya-Arunroj and Gail, 2019).
evidence: Stated with extensive citations to prior literature.

claim: Visuospatial neglect can be restricted to the near or far space as shown by patients with large-scale lesions comprising also parietal cortex.
source: Visuospatial neglect can be restricted to the near or far space as shown by patients with large-scale lesions comprising also parietal cortex (Halligan and Marshall, 1991; Vuilleumier et al., 1998) and transcranial magnetic stimulation over the parietal cortex (Bjoertomt et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to neuropsychological studies.

claim: Bimodal neurons in premotor cortex and the posterior parietal cortex of non-human primates respond to visual and somatosensory stimulation, with visual receptive fields being congruent with somatosensory receptive fields and thereby covering the space near the body.
source: Bimodal neurons in premotor cortex and the posterior parietal cortex of non-human primates respond to visual and somatosensory stimulation, with visual receptive fields being congruent with somatosensory receptive fields and thereby covering the space near the body (Colby and Goldberg, 1999; Graziano et al., 1997; Rizzolatti et al., 1981; Rizzolatti et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to neurophysiological studies.

claim: Mirror neurons in the ventral premotor cortex can respond differently to an observed reach if the reach goal is within its own reach or not.
source: In addition, mirror neurons in the ventral premotor cortex can respond differently to an observed reach if the reach goal is within its own reach or not. (Bonini et al., 2014; Caggiano et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on mirror neurons.

claim: Monkey K performed the final version of the walk-and-reach task with 77% correct trials on average.
source: Monkey K performed the final version of the walk-and-reach task (Figure 2A/B) with 77% correct trials on average (s.d. 9%, 19 sessions) with up to 412 correct trials per session (mean 208, s.d. 93).
evidence: Directly stated with specific performance metrics.

claim: Monkey L performed the final version of the task with 55% correct trials on average.
source: Monkey L performed the final version of the task with 55% correct trials on average (s.d. 5%, 10 sessions) with up to 326 correct trials per session (mean 219, s.d. 55).
evidence: Directly stated with specific performance metrics.

claim: Movement times were longer for far targets than for near targets in both monkeys.
source: As a whole-body translocation is required to approach far targets, movement times were longer than for near targets in both monkeys (t-test, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical testing of movement time distributions.

claim: Movement time distributions were narrow (s.d. ≤ 76 ms), indicating that the monkeys optimized their behavior for consistent target acquisition.
source: Movement time distributions were narrow (s.d. ≤ 76 ms), indicating that the monkeys optimized their behavior for consistent target acquisition.
evidence: Supported by measurement of movement time variability.

claim: The highest variability was seen in the wrist during walk-and-reach movements with a median of 37/46 mm and 0.75-quartile of 50/67 mm for monkeys K and L, respectively.
source: The highest variability was seen in the wrist during walk-and-reach movements with a median of 37/46 mm and 0.75-quartile of 50/67 mm for monkeys K and L, respectively.
evidence: Directly stated with specific measurements from kinematic analysis.

claim: Monkey K was sitting during the memory period and then used its left forelimb for walking and reaching.
source: Monkey K was sitting during the memory period and then used its left forelimb for walking and reaching.
evidence: Directly stated based on observation of movement patterns.

claim: Monkey L was standing during the memory period and walked bipedally to the far targets.
source: Monkey L was standing during the memory period and walked bipedally to the far targets.
evidence: Directly stated based on observation of movement patterns.

claim: Six 32-channel floating microwire arrays (FMA) with various lengths were chronically implanted in primary motor cortex (M1), dorsal premotor cortex (PMd), and the parietal reach region (PRR) in the posterior parietal cortex of both monkeys.
source: We chronically implanted a total of 192 electrodes in primary motor cortex (M1), dorsal premotor cortex (PMd), and the parietal reach region (PRR) in the posterior parietal cortex of both monkeys using six 32-channel floating microwire arrays (FMA) with various lengths (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Directly stated in the methods description.

claim: The wireless signal transmission was stable during walking movements with an average data loss rate of 3.32% (s.d. 1.7%) across sessions and monkeys.
source: On average across sessions and monkeys, the loss rate was 3.32% (s.d. 1.7%).
evidence: Directly stated with specific measurements of data loss.

claim: Three sessions revealed task-responsive activity on all 192 channels.
source: Three sessions revealed task-responsive activity on all 192 channels, that is showed at least one effect in distance, position, time, or one of the interactions; across all sessions the mean number of task-responsive channels was 189 (s.d. five channels).
evidence: Directly stated based on ANOVA analysis of neural activity.

claim: In PMd and PRR, decoding is significant for both memory and movement period for reach and walk-and-reach movements.
source: In PMd and PRR, decoding is significant for both memory and movement period for reach and walk-and-reach movements (Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by permutation test results on decoding accuracy.

claim: In M1, decoding accuracy only reached significance for walk-and-reach movements in monkey L during the movement period.
source: In M1, decoding accuracy only reached significance for walk-and-reach movements in monkey L during the movement period.
evidence: Supported by permutation test results on decoding accuracy.

claim: PMd and PRR show significant firing rate modulation for both memory and movement period for reach and walk-and-reach movements.
source: As in the decoding analysis, PMd and PRR show significant firing rate modulation for both memory and movement period for reach and walk-and-reach movements (Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by permutation test results on firing rate modulation.

claim: M1 shows significant firing rate modulation during the walk-and-reach movement period for both monkeys but not during the memory period.
source: Here, M1 shows significant firing rate modulation during the walk-and-reach movement period for both monkeys but, as for the decoding analysis, not during the memory period.
evidence: Supported by permutation test results on firing rate modulation.

claim: The decoding accuracy and firing rate modulation was not affected by the introduction of a passage that constrained walking paths, indicating independence from the movement path.
source: Although movement trajectories for the different motor goal locations collapsed onto very similar initial walking directions because of the passage (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), the decoding accuracy and firing rate modulation was not affected by this measure, that is was independent of the movement path (Figure 5 – figure supplement 1B and Figure 5—source data 3 and 4).
evidence: Supported by control experiment comparing trials with and without passage.

claim: PMd and PRR activity contains spatial information about the reach goal beyond the immediate reach.
source: This indicates that PRR and PMd activity contains spatial information about the reach goal beyond the immediate reach.
evidence: Inferred from decoding results showing target information during memory period for far targets, independent of walking path.

claim: PMd activity is known to encode reach related spatial information during planning of reaches within immediate reach.
source: PMd (e.g. Crammond and Kalaska, 1994) and PRR (e.g. Snyder et al., 1998) activity are known to encode reach related spatial information during planning of reaches within immediate reach.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PRR activity is known to encode reach related spatial information during planning of reaches within immediate reach.
source: PMd (e.g. Crammond and Kalaska, 1994) and PRR (e.g. Snyder et al., 1998) activity are known to encode reach related spatial information during planning of reaches within immediate reach.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The extent of the near space, often called peripersonal space, is variable.
source: The extent of the near space, often called peripersonal space (Rizzolatti et al., 1997), is variable.
evidence: Stated with citation to prior literature.

claim: Neurophysiological and neuropsychological studies have shown that peripersonal space can expand around tools.
source: Neurophysiological and neuropsychological studies have shown that it can expand around tools (Berti and Frassinetti, 2000; Giglia et al., 2015; Holmes, 2012; Iriki et al., 1996; Maravita et al., 2002; Maravita and Iriki, 2004) or fake arms (Blanke et al., 2015; Botvinick and Cohen, 1998; Graziano et al., 2000; Maravita et al., 2003; Pavani et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: There is evidence from human psychophysics that the peripersonal space expands towards reach goals.
source: There is evidence from human psychophysics that the peripersonal space, here defined by the spatial extent of visuo-tactile integration, expands towards reach goals (Brozzoli et al., 2009; Brozzoli et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to psychophysics studies.

claim: Peripersonal space in human participants expands to reach goals beyond immediate reach when subjects performed a walk-and-reach task similar to the one used in this study.
source: Correspondingly, we could show that peripersonal space, as defined by the occurrence of visuo-tactile integration, in human participants expands to reach goals beyond immediate reach when subjects performed a walk-and-reach task similar to here (Berger et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to authors' own prior work.

claim: None of the previous studies with neural recordings in unrestrained monkeys presented an experimental environment that instructs temporally and spatially precise movement behavior.
source: However, none of the experiments with neural recordings in unrestrained monkeys presented an experimental environment that instructs temporally and spatially precise movement behavior (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Stated with reference to supplementary comparison table.

claim: The MCT cylinder has a diameter of 75 mm and a length of 160 mm.
source: The MCT cylinder is made of PVC plastic and has a diameter of 75 mm and a length of 160 mm.
evidence: Directly stated in the technical description.

claim: The MCTs contain a capacitive proximity sensor and four RGB-LEDs.
source: At one end of the cylinder the MCTs contain a capacitive proximity sensor (EC3016NPAPL, Carlo Gavazzi, Steinhausen, Switzerland) and four RGB-LEDs (WS2812B, Worldsemi Co., Daling Village, China), both protected behind a clear polycarbonate cover.
evidence: Directly stated in the technical description.

claim: The Reach Cage inner dimensions are 170 cm x 80 cm x 85 cm (W x D x H).
source: Inner cage dimensions are 170 cm x 80 cm x 85 cm (W x D x H) with a metal mesh grid at the top and bottom, a solid metal wall on one long side (back), and clear polycarbonate walls on all other sides.
evidence: Directly stated in the technical description.

claim: The near targets were placed with a 10 cm horizontal distance and 60 cm vertical distance to the starting position.
source: The row of ceiling MCTs closer to the starting position was placed with a 10 cm horizontal distance and 60 cm vertical distance to the starting position (near targets).
evidence: Directly stated in the experimental setup description.

claim: The far targets were positioned at 100 cm horizontal distance from the starting positions.
source: The second row of MCTs was positioned at 100 cm horizontal distance from the starting positions (far targets) requiring the animal to make steps towards the targets (Figure 2B).
evidence: Directly stated in the experimental setup description.

claim: Both animals learned within a single first session that touching a target presented on an MCT leads to a liquid reward.
source: Both animals learned within a single first session that touching a target presented on a MaCaQuE Cue and Target box (MCT, Figure 1B) leads to a liquid reward.
evidence: Directly stated based on training observations.

claim: The majority of errors resulted from premature release of the start buttons prior to the go cue.
source: The majority of errors resulted from premature release of the start buttons prior to the go cue.
evidence: Directly stated based on error analysis.

claim: Trials with properly timed movement initiation were 92% correct in monkey K and 78% correct in monkey L.
source: Trials with properly timed movement initiation were 92% correct in monkey K and 78% correct in monkey L.
evidence: Directly stated based on behavioral analysis.

claim: DeepLabCut provides excellent tracking of body parts from different species such as monkeys, mice, flies, humans, fish, horses, and cheetahs.
source: DeepLabCut provides excellent tracking of body parts from different species such as monkeys (Labuguen et al., 2019), mice, flies, humans, fish, horses, and cheetahs (Nath et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to DeepLabCut publications.

claim: The root mean squared error for body part tracking was 2.57 pixels for the training data and 4.7 pixels for test data.
source: For the remaining data points of all 10 features, the root mean squared error was 2.57 pixels for the training and 4.7 pixels for test data.
evidence: Directly stated based on cross-validation analysis of DeepLabCut tracking.

claim: After rejecting all outliers, the percentage of valid data points during correctly performed trials for Monkey K/L was: wrist 94.93%; elbow 92.51%; shoulder 94.98%; headcap 97.58%.
source: After rejecting all outliers (DeepLabCut low likelihood, reprojection error, boundary box, and discontinuity), the percentage of valid data points of all seven analyzed sessions during correctly performed trials for Monkey K/L was: wrist 94.93%; elbow 92.51%; shoulder 94.98%; headcap 97.58%.
evidence: Directly stated based on motion capture data quality analysis.

claim: The chamber was milled out of polyether ether ketone (TECAPEEK) to be lightweight and biocompatible.
source: The chamber was milled out of polyether ether ketone (TECAPEEK, Ensinger GmbH, Nufringen, Germany) to be lightweight (monkey K/L: 10/14 grams; 65/60.3 mm max. length, 50/49.5 mm max. width, 24.9/31.2 mm max. height; wall thickness: 2/2 mm) and biocompatible.
evidence: Directly stated in the implant design description.

claim: Six 32-channel floating microelectrode arrays were implanted in the right hemisphere of both monkeys.
source: We implanted six FMAs in the right hemisphere of both monkeys.
evidence: Directly stated in the surgical procedure description.

claim: PRR arrays were positioned along the medial wall of the intraparietal sulcus (IPS) starting about 7 mm away from the parieto-occipital sulcus, with electrode lengths of 1.5–7.1 mm.
source: PRR arrays were positioned along the medial wall of the intraparietal sulcus (IPS) starting about 7 mm away from the parieto-occipital sulcus (Figure 6B), with electrode lengths of 1.5–7.1 mm.
evidence: Directly stated in the surgical procedure description.

claim: M1 arrays were positioned along the frontal wall of the central sulcus, at a laterality between precentral dimple and arcuate spur, with electrode lengths of 1.5–7.1 mm.
source: M1 arrays were positioned along the frontal wall of the central sulcus, at a laterality between precentral dimple and arcuate spur, with electrode lengths of 1.5–7.1 mm.
evidence: Directly stated in the surgical procedure description.

claim: PMd arrays were positioned between arcuate spur, precentral dimple, and the M1 arrays as close to the arcuate spur, with electrode lengths of 1.9–4.5 mm.
source: PMd arrays were positioned, between arcuate spur, precentral dimple, and the M1 arrays as close to the arcuate spur, with electrode lengths of 1.9–4.5 mm.
evidence: Directly stated in the surgical procedure description.

claim: 192 channels is the highest channel count of recording full broadband (30 ksps per channel) intracortical recordings in unrestrained non-human primates to the authors' knowledge.
source: To our knowledge, 192 channels is the highest channel count of recording full broadband (30 ksps per channel) intracortical recordings in unrestrained non-human primates.
evidence: Stated as a claim about the state of the field based on authors' knowledge.

claim: Previous studies presented simultaneous recordings of 96 channels broadband data in unrestrained primates.
source: Previous studies presented simultaneous recordings of 96 channels broadband data; when higher channel counts were used, for example spiking activity from 512 channels (Schwarz et al., 2014), automatic spike detection on the headstage was applied and only spike times and waveforms were transmitted and recorded.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Goal-directed behavior might lead to an expansion of peripersonal space even beyond immediate reach.
source: While previous research suggested selective encoding of near space in parts of parietal and premotor cortex, goal-directed behavior might lead to an expansion of so-called near space even beyond immediate reach.
evidence: Proposed as an explanation for the observed far-space encoding.

claim: Far-located walk-and-reach goals might effectively be within the 'near space' and be encoded similar to near-located reach goals in parietal and premotor regions known for reach goal selectivity during planning and movement.
source: Far-located walk-and-reach goals hence might effectively be within the 'near space' and be encoded similar to near-located reach goals in parietal and premotor regions known for reach goal selectivity during planning and movement.
evidence: Proposed as a speculative explanation for the findings.

claim: The Reach Cage allows systems-level sensorimotor neuroscience studies with full-body movements in a configurable 3D spatial setting with unrestrained monkeys.
source: The Reach Cage allows systems-level sensorimotor neuroscience studies with full-body movements in a configurable 3D spatial setting with unrestrained monkeys.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion based on the demonstrated capabilities of the system.

claim: The Reach Cage is suitable for sensorimotor neuroscience with physically unrestrained rhesus monkeys providing a richer set of motor tasks, including walk-and-reach movements.
source: We show that the Reach Cage is suitable for sensorimotor neuroscience with physically unrestrained rhesus monkeys providing a richer set of motor tasks, including walk-and-reach movements.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion based on the behavioral and neural data collected.

claim: The Reach Cage environment allows studying sensorimotor neuroscience questions within an unrestrained spatial setting.
source: Taken together, the Reach Cage environment allows us to study sensorimotor neuroscience questions within an unrestrained spatial setting.
evidence: Stated as a summary conclusion.

claim: Target location information is present in premotor and parietal cortex of far-located targets beyond the immediate reach.
source: Here, we show that target location information is present in premotor and parietal cortex of far-located targets beyond the immediate reach.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion based on decoding and encoding analyses.

claim: Intracortical signals can be decoded to control external devices, as demonstrated in non-human primates.
source: Intracortical signals can be decoded to control external devices, as demonstrated in non-human primates (Carmena, 2013; Hauschild et al., 2012; Musallam et al., 2004; Santhanam et al., 2006; Serruya et al., 2002; Taylor, 2002; Velliste et al., 2008; Wessberg et al., 2000), and suited to partially restore motor function in quadriplegic human patients (Aflalo et al., 2015; Bouton et al., 2016; Collinger et al., 2013; Gilja et al., 2015; Hochberg et al., 2012; Wodlinger et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by extensive citations to BMI literature.

claim: When monkeys perform an arm movement task in parallel to a BMI cursor task based on decoding arm movement related neural activity, the BMI performance decreases.
source: A previous study showed that when monkeys perform an arm movement task in parallel to a BMI cursor task based on decoding arm movement related neural activity, the BMI performance decreases (Orsborn et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: The recording bandwidth and quality is sufficiently high for analyzing neural spiking activity in multiple brain areas simultaneously.
source: We show that our recording bandwidth and quality is sufficiently high for analyzing neural spiking activity in multiple brain areas simultaneously.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion based on the neural recording results.

claim: There is enough information in the population activity to be detected by a decoder on a single trial basis.
source: Further, we show that there is enough information in the population activity to be detected by a decoder on a single trial basis.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion based on decoding analysis.

claim: MaCaQuE was also used successfully in a study with human participants.
source: Here we report the technical details of MaCaQuE and its use with physically unrestrained rhesus monkeys; however, we also used MaCaQuE successfully in a study with human participants (Berger et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to authors' own work.

claim: All procedures have been approved by the responsible regional government office under permit numbers 3392 42502-04-13/1100 and comply with German Law and the European Directive 2010/63/EU regulating use of animals in research.
source: All procedures have been approved by the responsible regional government office [Niedersächsisches Landesamt für Verbraucherschutz und Lebensmittelsicherheit (LAVES)] under permit numbers 3392 42502-04-13/1100 and comply with German Law and the European Directive 2010/63/EU regulating use of animals in research.
evidence: Directly stated in the ethics statement.
